title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in SwaggerUI via Unsanitized Request Path in Inline Script
analysis:
- Source: Untrusted HTTP request path `call.request.path()`, which is directly read from the request URI (e.g. `origin.uri.substringBefore('?')`).
- Sanitization/Validation: None. The path is directly string-interpolated into an `unsafe { ... }` block inside an HTML `<script>` element without any HTML escaping or JavaScript string sanitization.
- Sink: `call.respondHtml` outputs the raw HTML containing the unescaped `<script>` block in the HTTP response.
- Reachability & Conceptual Exploit Payload:
When `swaggerUI` is installed under a path that includes a route parameter, wildcard, or regex (e.g. `route("api/{version}") { swaggerUI("swagger") }` or `swaggerUI("{tenant}/docs")`), an attacker can send an HTTP request with an XSS payload in the path:
`GET /api/</script><script>alert(document.domain)</script>/swagger HTTP/1.1`
`Host: example.com`

The route matches, and `call.request.path()` returns `/api/</script><script>alert(document.domain)</script>/swagger`.
The response contains:
```html
<script>window.onload = function() {
    window.ui = SwaggerUIBundle({
        url: '/api/</script><script>alert(document.domain)</script>/swagger/documentation.yaml',
...
```
When the victim browser parses this HTML, the `</script>` tag closes the script block prematurely and `<script>alert(document.domain)</script>` executes in the victim's origin, enabling Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

title: Access Control Bypass in staticFiles via Directory Index and Fallback Path
analysis:
- Source: Untrusted HTTP GET request to a static file directory served using `staticFiles` (or `singlePageApplication`).
- Sanitization/Validation: In `StaticContent.kt`, the developer can configure an `exclude` predicate to forbid access to specific files (returning 403 Forbidden). However, `checkExclude` is ONLY called inside the `else if (!isDirectory)` block. When a requested path resolves to a directory (`requestedFile.isDirectory == true`), line 463 executes:
`if (index != null && isDirectory) { respondStaticFile(File(requestedFile, index), ...) }`
Neither `requestedFile` nor `File(requestedFile, index)` is checked against `checkExclude`. In addition, line 480 serves `File(dir, defaultPath)` without checking `checkExclude`.
- Sink: `respondStaticFile` / `LocalFileContent` reads and serves the excluded file contents with status 200 OK.
- Reachability & Conceptual Exploit Payload:
Consider a route configured as:
```kotlin
routing {
    staticFiles("/static", File("/var/www/static")) {
        exclude { file -> file.path.contains("admin") || file.name == "index.html" }
    }
}
```
A direct request to `GET /static/admin/index.html` is blocked and returns `403 Forbidden`.
However, an attacker sends:
`GET /static/admin/ HTTP/1.1`
`Host: example.com`

Because `/static/admin/` resolves to directory `/var/www/static/admin`, `requestedFile.isDirectory` evaluates to `true`. Line 463 matches and immediately invokes `respondStaticFile(File(requestedFile, index), ...)` without running `checkExclude`. The protected index file `/var/www/static/admin/index.html` is returned with `200 OK`, bypassing the authorization policy.

title: CBC Padding Oracle and Non-Constant-Time MAC Verification in SessionTransportTransformerEncrypt
analysis:
- Source: Untrusted session cookie/header value provided in HTTP requests (`transportValue`).
- Sanitization/Validation: `SessionTransportTransformerEncrypt` uses an "Encrypt-and-MAC" scheme with AES-CBC and PKCS#5 padding (`$encryptAlgorithm/CBC/PKCS5PADDING`). In `transformRead`, it performs `decrypt(iv, encrypted)` BEFORE validating the HMAC signature (`hex(mac(decrypted)) != macHex`). Additionally, the HMAC verification uses standard string comparison (`!=`) instead of constant-time comparison (`MessageDigest.isEqual`), creating timing side-channels.
- Sink: `Cipher.doFinal(input)` is invoked on unauthenticated ciphertext, throwing `BadPaddingException` on invalid padding.
- Reachability & Conceptual Exploit Payload:
An attacker intercepts an encrypted session cookie:
`Cookie: SESSION=0102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f10/616263...:8f2a...`
The attacker modifies the ciphertext bytes and sends manipulated cookies to the server. If the modified ciphertext produces invalid PKCS#5 padding, `Cipher.doFinal` immediately fails with a padding exception; if it produces valid padding, decryption succeeds and the server proceeds to compute and compare the MAC. This differential timing / padding oracle allows an adversary to decrypt arbitrary session data without knowing the AES encryption key.
